v.why: Replacing a dead final edge with a conv restores a path to the output, a larger gain than swapping one working op for another.
Filling a removed edge with a conv adds capacity and a feature path, which gives more than upgrading an existing op.
Activating an empty direct input-to-output edge with a conv gives a larger gain than replacing an existing op.
Edge 0 feeds node 1, so a conv there reconnects a whole branch of the cell.
Adding a skip where the edge was absent improves gradient flow far more than replacing an op that was already working.
Deleting a conv on the final edge removes the strongest op and costs much more than deleting a weak op.
Removing a conv edge into the output costs more accuracy than removing a pool or a skip.
Gains saturate when another strong conv already feeds the output node.
A second conv into the output is redundant when edge 5 already provides one.
Removing the direct edge costs little when a strong conv path into the output remains, so the effect is less negative.
Removing edge 3 hurts more when edge 5 is already absent, because it removes a main remaining route to the output.
With edge 5 absent, deleting edge 4 cuts another path to the output and is more damaging.
Node 2 already receives a strong conv from edge 1, so a second conv into it adds less.
With edge 0 absent, edge 1 is the only source of node 2's features, so upgrading it matters more.
With edge 1 absent, node 2 carries less information, so a conv on edge 5 gains less.
Any non-zero op on an empty direct edge helps, while replacing a conv or skip with a pool does not.
Reconnecting node 1 with a skip is a large gain over a dead edge but not over a working op.
A second skip into the output is redundant with the one on edge 3.
Two skip paths into the output substitute for each other, so the added skip gains less.
Removing a conv on the inner edge loses more than removing a weaker op.

I had no retrieved abstracts to draw on, so these hypotheses rest on well-known NAS-Bench-201 regularities. Nothing was checked against benchmark data. The regularities used are:
- Replacing a `none` edge gains the most.
- Removing a conv edge costs a lot.
- Gains saturate when a parallel strong path already exists.
- Dropping the only remaining path to the output is especially harmful.
